newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Failed round-world balloonist says feared fumes.
newsitem.headline: Failed round-world balloonist says feared fumes.

text.p: Swiss balloonist Bertrand Piccard said on Monday he had called off a bid to fly round the world on Sunday because he and his co-pilot feared they would be totally overcome by escaping fuel fumes.

Piccard, whose Breitling Orbiter ditched in the Mediterranean after only six hours aloft, told Swiss radio the pair had decided before they took off that they would take no risks if there were any sign of danger.

Cutting short the flight so soon was "a terribly difficult decision to take", said the 38-year-old psychiatrist, whose father and grandfather are both in world record books for exploration of the stratosphere and the ocean depths.
"But our eyes were stinging and our throats were hurting. We felt we were going to be totally overwhelmed by the fumes.
"On top of that, we both have families and had set out out to do this (fly round the world) in a totally rational way," he said.

Flight controllers said on Sunday the decision to abort the mission, planned to last between 15 and 20 days and make use of east-blowing jet-stream winds around the globe, followed leakage of kerosene fumes into the Orbiter's bright yellow, pressurised cabin.
It was not clear if the fumes came from the capsule's heating system or from the burners which were to keep the giant, helium-filled balloon aloft during hours of darkness.
Flying with Piccard was 39-year-old Belgian businessman and professional pilot Wim Verstraeten. The pair had often flown together, winning the first trans-Atlantic balloon race in 1992.

Both were pronounced well by French doctors after being lifted from the sea by a coastguard launch. British mission director Alan Noble said on Sunday if the balloon and capsule were in good shape they could be used for another bid.
Piccard said it was decided to come down in the sea rather than on land to ensure minimum damage to the British-built Orbiter and the crew's cabin.

The craft had taken off in blue skies and perfect weather conditions early on Sunday from the Swiss Alpine ballooning centre of Chateau d'Oex. But the trouble developed just three hours into the flight.

No manned air balloon has ever stayed aloft for more than five days. The failure of the Orbiter came less than a week after British businessman Richard Branson called off a similar bid within 24 hours of lift-off from Morocco.
An American millionaire enthusiast, Steve Fosset, is due to take off within the next few days from St Louis, Missouri, in his second bid to become the first man to circle the globe on a balloon.
Branson, who went to Chateau d'Oex to see Piccard and Verstraeten off and then followed them some of the way in his private jet, said he would probably now make another attempt in November this year.
